note: AI-ONLY source of truth. Contains answers. Learners: reading this defeats your own learning.

questions.prompt: A SOC analyst's main job is to:

options.B: Watch for suspicious activity, decide if it is real, and respond

questions.why: A SOC detects, decides and responds to security events.

questions.prompt: In the mall-security analogy, 'it was just a cat that set off the alarm' is a:

options.B: False positive

questions.why: An alert about something harmless is a false positive.

questions.prompt: Which is an INTERNAL threat?

options.B: An employee copying sensitive files to a personal cloud drive

questions.why: Internal threats come from people or accounts inside the organisation, accidental or deliberate.

questions.prompt: When you are unsure whether an alert is serious, a new analyst should:

options.A: Close it to keep the queue clean
options.B: Ignore it

questions.why: When unsure, escalate with facts. Never guess silently.

questions.prompt: Which OSI layer deals with IP addresses and routing?

options.B: Layer 3

questions.why: Layer 3 is the Network layer.

questions.prompt: Which port does RDP (Remote Desktop) use by default?
questions.why: RDP uses TCP 3389.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of the TCP 3-way handshake?

options.B: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK

questions.why: Client SYN, server SYN-ACK, client ACK.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a private (RFC1918) range?
Which log records SSH logins on Ubuntu/Debian?

options.B: /var/log/auth.log

questions.why: auth.log holds authentication events.

questions.prompt: Which command lets you watch a log file update live?

options.B: tail -f file.log

questions.why: tail -f follows the end of the file.

questions.prompt: A cron job that runs a script from /tmp every 5 minutes, added by a non-admin user, most likely suggests:

options.B: Persistence by an attacker

questions.why: Scripts in /tmp scheduled by unexpected users are a classic persistence sign.

questions.prompt: Ransomware that encrypts files so nobody can use them mainly breaks which part of the CIA triad?

options.B: Integrity

questions.why: Availability: the data can't be used.

questions.prompt: In the Kill Chain, malware setting up a way to survive reboots is:

options.B: Exploitation

questions.why: Installation is where persistence is planted.

questions.prompt: Which is an IOA (behaviour) rather than an IOC (static clue)?

options.B: Word starting PowerShell that downloads a file

questions.why: IOAs describe behaviour in progress.

questions.prompt: Which indicator is hardest for an attacker to change?

options.B: IP addresses

questions.why: TTPs sit at the top of the pyramid.

questions.prompt: First action on a machine with active ransomware:

options.B: Isolate it from the network, don't power off unless told to

questions.why: Isolation stops spread and preserves memory evidence.

questions.prompt: A user typed their password into a fake login page. A good first step is to:

options.B: Reset the password and revoke active sessions
options.C: Tell the user to ignore it

questions.why: Credentials are compromised; reset and revoke sessions.

questions.prompt: Before talking to an employee suspected of misusing data, you should:

options.B: Involve HR/management per policy and preserve evidence
options.D: Post about it in a team chat

questions.why: Insider cases need HR/management coordination and careful evidence handling.

questions.prompt: A good ticket note contains:

options.B: What fired, what you checked, what you found, what you did, and the next step

questions.why: Notes must let a stranger follow your work.

questions.prompt: A ticket was closed as 'false positive', but the IP now matches fresh threat intel as a known command server. You should:

options.B: Reopen it, present the evidence and re-review

questions.why: New context means re-reviewing.

questions.prompt: You see what looks like confirmed ransomware (Critical). As L1 you should:

options.B: Escalate immediately and contain within your authority
options.C: Wait until the end of your shift
options.D: Ask a friend on social media

questions.why: Critical incidents need immediate escalation.

questions.prompt: Which IOC type is the LEAST durable?

options.B: TTP

questions.why: Hashes change with a single byte.

questions.prompt: Which is a correctly 'defanged' URL?

options.B: hxxp://bad-site[.]example/login

questions.why: Defanging replaces http with hxxp and '.' with '[.]'.

questions.prompt: A mutex IOC is:

options.B: A name malware creates to mark a host as already infected

questions.why: Malware uses mutex names to avoid double infection.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of a SIEM?

options.B: Collect and normalise logs from many sources, correlate them and raise alerts

questions.why: A SIEM centralises logs, makes them comparable, detects patterns and alerts.

questions.prompt: What does EDR 'host isolation' do?

options.B: Cuts the machine off from the network but keeps the EDR link

questions.why: You can still investigate while it is cut off.

questions.prompt: Windows Event ID 4625 means:

options.B: Failed logon

questions.why: 4624 is success, 4625 is failure.

questions.prompt: Your SIEM dashboard suddenly shows almost no events from the firewall. The best first thought is:

options.B: Check whether the log source or collector stopped reporting

questions.why: Silence can mean a broken collector or an attacker hiding. Check source health first.

questions.prompt: CERT-In's directions require reporting listed incidents within:

options.B: 6 hours

questions.why: Six hours from noticing.

questions.prompt: CERT-In requires logs of ICT systems to be kept for a rolling:

options.B: 90 days

questions.why: 180 days, within Indian jurisdiction.

questions.prompt: Under the DPDP Rules, the detailed personal data breach report to the Data Protection Board is due within:

options.B: 24 hours

questions.why: 72 hours (after an initial intimation without delay).

questions.prompt: Which of these is a certifiable AI management system standard?

options.B: ISO/IEC 42001

questions.prompt: Which function did NIST CSF 2.0 add to the original five?

options.B: Recover

questions.why: Govern.

questions.objective: Know who SEBI CSCRF is for
questions.prompt: SEBI's CSCRF mainly applies to:

options.B: SEBI-regulated securities-market entities

questions.why: Brokers, exchanges, depositories, fund houses and similar entities.

questions.prompt: 'Data poisoning' means:

options.B: Feeding bad data so an AI learns the wrong thing

questions.why: Corrupting training data.

questions.prompt: You notice a possible reportable incident. The best habit is to:

options.A: Wait and watch for an hour
options.B: Record the exact time you noticed and escalate
options.D: Report directly to the regulator yourself

questions.why: The clock runs from noticing; escalate to those who file.

questions.prompt: MITRE ATT&CK is best described as:

options.B: A public catalogue of attacker tactics and techniques

questions.why: A knowledge base of adversary behaviour.

questions.prompt: Explain to a friend, using a simple analogy, what a SOC does and who it protects against.
rubric: Uses a sensible analogy (control room, guards, CCTV)
Mentions detect, respond and improve
Names external and internal threats
Plain language, no jargon dump

questions.prompt: A host sends DNS queries to random-looking subdomains of an unfamiliar domain every few seconds. What might this be and what would you check?
rubric: Suggests DNS tunnelling or command-and-control beaconing
Checks domain age/reputation and query pattern
Looks at the host's other activity
Correlates with proxy/firewall logs and escalates if suspicious

questions.prompt: auth.log shows about 200 failed SSH logins from one IP followed by one success. What do you do?
rubric: Treats the success as possibly compromised
Reviews what the session did (history, processes, connections)
Blocks or rate-limits the source
Resets the account, considers MFA, checks other accounts, escalates with notes

questions.prompt: Give one example of an IOC and one of an IOA, and explain why behaviour-based detection lasts longer.
rubric: Valid IOC example (hash, IP, domain)
Valid IOA example (behaviour sequence)
Explains attackers can change IOCs easily but not habits (Pyramid of Pain)

questions.prompt: A user says they clicked a link and entered their password on a page that looked slightly wrong. Walk through your first steps.
rubric: Resets password / revokes sessions
Checks recent sign-ins for the account
Blocks the URL/domain
Finds other recipients of the email
Notifies and documents

questions.prompt: Write a ticket note for: 'Antivirus quarantined a file on a finance laptop; the process is still running.'
rubric: Includes what fired, who/what, what was checked
States facts, not guesses
Says the issue is not resolved because the process still runs
Lists actions (isolate if authorised) and next steps/escalation

questions.prompt: You find the address http://bad-site.example/login and the IP 203.0.113.45. Defang them, classify each IOC type, and say which lasts longer.
rubric: Defangs correctly (hxxp, [.])
Classifies URL/domain and IPv4
Notes IPs/URLs are short-lived and behaviour lasts longer

questions.prompt: EDR shows Word launching PowerShell with an encoded command. How would you use the SIEM, EDR and firewall/log analyzer together?
rubric: Uses EDR process tree/storyline
Searches SIEM for network connections/related events from the host
Checks firewall/log analyzer for allowed/blocked outbound traffic
Builds one timeline, isolates if malicious, escalates and documents

questions.prompt: At 3 AM you notice a server uploading customer data to an unknown address. Describe your first 30 minutes and which legal clocks may start.
rubric: Records exact time noticed
Isolates the host if authorised, doesn't power off or delete logs
Escalates quickly
States personal data may be involved
Names CERT-In 6 hours and DPDP 72 hours as possible clocks (compliance decides)

questions.prompt: Windows Event ID 4688 records:

options.B: A new process being created

questions.why: 4688 is process creation (when auditing is enabled).

questions.prompt: A logon of type 10 usually means:

options.B: A scheduled task

questions.why: Type 10 is RemoteInteractive, i.e. RDP.

questions.prompt: Kerberoasting is when an attacker:

options.A: Floods a server with SYN packets
options.B: Requests service tickets for service accounts and cracks them offline
options.C: Encrypts files on a file server

questions.why: It targets service-account passwords through their Kerberos tickets.

questions.prompt: Event ID 1102 on a server tells you:

options.B: A scheduled task was created
options.C: The security audit log was cleared

questions.why: Clearing the log is a classic attempt to hide tracks.

questions.prompt: At 2 AM a server shows its security log cleared (1102) and a new member added to the local administrators group. What do you do?
rubric: Treats it as high severity and escalates quickly
Checks who did it (account, logon type, source) and the time
Looks for other changes: new accounts, services, scheduled tasks, process creations
Preserves evidence, does not 'fix' it silently, isolates the host if authorised
Documents times and facts clearly

questions.prompt: An IPS differs from an IDS because it:

options.B: Sits in the traffic path and can block

questions.why: An IPS is inline and can prevent traffic as well as alert.

questions.prompt: Thousands of SYN packets with very few completed handshakes most likely indicate:

options.B: A SYN flood (denial of service attempt)

questions.why: Half-open connections piling up is the SYN flood signature.

questions.prompt: A host connects to the same outside address every 60 seconds with tiny amounts of data. This pattern suggests:

options.B: A large download

questions.why: Regular, small, repeated connections are typical of malware check-ins.

questions.prompt: Why are network metadata or flow logs often more useful than full packet capture for everyday work?

options.A: They contain every byte of content
options.B: They're small enough to keep longer and show who talked to whom, even when traffic is encrypted

questions.why: Metadata is cheaper to store and still reveals behaviour.

questions.prompt: An IDS alerts on SSH brute-force attempts from an external IP against a Linux server. Describe what you check and do.
rubric: Checks whether any login succeeded (auth log)
Looks at volume, timing and other targeted hosts
Checks the source reputation and whether SSH should be exposed
Blocks or rate-limits the source within authority
Escalates if there was a success, with notes

questions.prompt: A rule that fires when many failed logins are followed by a success from the same source is a:

options.B: Sequence / correlation rule

questions.why: It links related events in order.

questions.prompt: Sigma is best described as:

options.B: A product-neutral format for writing log detections

questions.why: Sigma rules can be translated for many SIEMs.

questions.prompt: A threat hunt should begin with:

options.B: A hypothesis about attacker behaviour

questions.why: Hunts are hypothesis-driven.

questions.prompt: Why do teams tune detections?

options.B: To cut false positives so real alerts get attention, without missing real attacks

questions.why: Tuning keeps alerts useful.

questions.prompt: Sketch a detection for 'off-hours privileged login': data source, logic, severity, likely false positives and first response steps.
rubric: Names a suitable log source (auth/identity logs)
Defines logic (admin account, outside normal hours or new location)
Assigns a sensible severity (high)
Lists plausible false positives (on-call work, maintenance)
Gives first steps (verify with owner, check session activity, escalate)

questions.prompt: In the four-phase NIST (Rev. 2) model, containment, eradication and recovery belong to:

options.B: Phase 2

questions.why: Phase 3 is Containment, Eradication and Recovery.

questions.prompt: A good 'lessons learned' review is:

options.A: A search for who to blame
options.B: A blameless review that improves process and detections

questions.why: Fix systems and process, not people.

questions.prompt: When explaining an incident to a non-technical manager you should lead with:

options.B: Impact, what is being done, and when the next update is

questions.why: Use Situation, Impact, Action, Next.

questions.prompt: In April 2025 NIST replaced SP 800-61 Rev. 2 with Rev. 3, which organises incident response around:

options.B: The six NIST CSF 2.0 functions

questions.why: Rev. 3 is a CSF 2.0 community profile.

questions.prompt: Write a four-sentence update for a manager: ransomware was found on three laptops and has been contained. Use Situation, Impact, Action, Next.
rubric: Situation stated plainly without jargon
Impact: three laptops, what is and isn't known about data
Action: isolation and steps taken
Next: checks under way and a time for the next update
Does not speculate or blame

questions.prompt: A SOAR playbook is:

options.B: Automated or semi-automated response steps for a type of alert

questions.why: Playbooks automate repeatable steps with guard-rails.

questions.prompt: Before uploading a suspicious file from your company to a public online sandbox you should:

options.B: Check whether it contains confidential data and use approved private tools, or look up only the hash

questions.why: Many public services share submissions.

questions.prompt: Why require human approval before high-impact automated actions?

options.B: To avoid isolating critical systems or blocking critical partners by mistake

questions.why: Guard-rails prevent costly false positives.

questions.prompt: STIX and TAXII are:

options.B: Standards for formatting and sharing threat intelligence

questions.why: STIX is the format; TAXII is the transport.

questions.prompt: Threat intelligence flags an IP that belongs to one of your vendors. Describe your process.
rubric: Checks the source and confidence of the intel
Checks whether traffic with that vendor is expected and the recent activity
Does not auto-block a critical partner
Contacts the owner or vendor contact through the proper channel
Documents and escalates if unclear

questions.prompt: In the cloud shared responsibility model, YOU are usually responsible for:

options.B: Your identities, configuration and data

questions.why: The provider secures the cloud; you secure what you put in it.

questions.prompt: A vulnerability with a CVSS score of 9.8 is rated:

options.B: Medium

questions.why: 9.0 to 10.0 is Critical.

questions.prompt: UEBA mainly works by:

options.B: Learning normal behaviour and flagging unusual behaviour

questions.why: It baselines users and entities.

questions.prompt: A cloud storage bucket that has been made public is mainly a risk of:

options.B: Data exposure to the internet

questions.why: Public buckets leak data.

questions.prompt: A critical vulnerability is announced in software that your company runs on an internet-facing server. What does the SOC check and do?
rubric: Confirms whether the software and version are in use
Checks exposure (internet-facing) and exploitation status
Looks for exploit attempts in logs and IDS/WAF
Coordinates with the owner on patch or mitigation
Increases monitoring and documents

questions.objective: Explain why missing logs are not good news
questions.prompt: You can't find any endpoint logs for an alerting laptop. The safest way to read that is:

options.A: Nothing happened, so close the alert
options.B: The silence itself needs explaining: a coverage, retention or agent problem may be hiding activity

questions.why: Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence. Find out why the data is missing.

questions.prompt: A strong 'insufficient evidence' answer includes:

options.A: The words 'need more info' and nothing else
options.B: Specific missing data, how each finding would change the decision, a safe interim action and a review time
options.C: A guess about who the attacker is
options.D: A request to close the ticket

questions.why: Specifics, decision impact, safe interim action and a review time make the answer useful.

questions.prompt: A server may be uploading sensitive data but you can't yet tell if it's approved. The best interim step is to:

options.A: Close the alert as a probable backup
options.B: Power off and wipe the server
options.C: Contact the owner, preserve the logs, check tickets and keep the alert open with a short review time

questions.why: Gather facts fast and preserve evidence without destructive action.

questions.prompt: The EDR shows a full malicious process chain, a malicious domain confirmed by several sources and a new scheduled task. Answering 'insufficient evidence' would be:

options.B: Over-cautious, because it delays containment when the evidence already answers the question
options.D: A good way to reduce workload

questions.why: Strong evidence means act. Judgment includes knowing when you already have enough.

questions.prompt: An alert shows a possible phishing click, but the email gateway no longer holds the message and proxy logs only cover the last 24 hours. Write a short ticket note that records what you know, what you don't know, how each finding would change your decision, and your safe next step.
rubric: States known facts separately from unknowns
Names specific missing data (original email, proxy and sign-in logs) and where to get it
Explains how findings would change the verdict
Chooses a safe interim action and sets a review time
Doesn't close prematurely or claim a confirmed breach
